newsitem.title: USA: New York Senate sees $922 mln in extra revenues.
newsitem.headline: New York Senate sees $922 mln in extra revenues.

text.p: The New York State Senate on Monday projected that the state would get an extra $922 million of tax revenues by the end of the 1998 fiscal year, nearly one-third more than Gov. George Pataki forecast.

And Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, also looks for the state to collect a fatter surplus during the 1997 fiscal year, which ends March 31. He projected a $1.7 billion surplus, about $100 million more than Pataki.

"This positive economic forecast is proof that our policies of cutting taxes, holding down spending and removing regulations is working to strengthen our state's economy," Bruno said, in prepared remarks. Calculating that over the past three years, New York State had cut over $5.9 billion in taxes, he noted that the state also had a surplus in the 1996 fiscal year, though it was only $445 million.

The Senate, whose revenue estimates fell short of those anticipated from the Democrat-led Assembly, urged that the windfall be used to pay for its plan to cut school property taxes as well as more reductions in business taxes, including the Gross Receipts Tax, which it said drives up the state's energy costs.

The Assembly, which was expected to forecast that tax collections would surge above initial estimates by as much as $2 billion from now until the end of the 1998 fiscal year, has said its main priorities for the huge windfall are education, higher education, and health care.

The state's revenues are projected to rise sharply mainly because Wall Street banks and brokerages are forecast to have another strong year of earnings. They raked in an estimated $11.5 billion in calender year 1996.

Pataki, in his fiscal 1998 budget, proposed slashing Medicaid spending by $900 million, though he later said he would restore $100 million of those cutbacks. The Republican governor's plans to raise tuition at state colleges also have been criticized.
Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, was slated to soon disclose his precise estimates, and the Assembly and the Senate will work together to develop a consensus estimate.

Bruno said the Senate would consider spending some of the extra funds on two of the Assembly's priorities, saying "We will also take a close look at restoring funds for health care programs and higher education."
